---
title: "Reporting, allocation and classification"
subtitle: "3.13 · constructed examples after the postrank theory book, ch. 17 and 19"
description: "Distinct objectives for pairwise reporting, place allocation and threshold classification."
---

Selecting the largest posterior expected value differs from selecting the most probable first-ranked unit.
A grade report instead determines which pairwise directions to state. The examples evaluate these objectives under
one law. Allocation from shared grades requires a further selection rule. Threshold classification depends on
exceedance probabilities and false-positive and false-negative costs. Grades alone specify neither decision.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Three units, reporting objective.** The report has risk .1833. Filling a place from its highest grade selects
  expected value 4.000 and has top-set overlap .700. The marked native-objective point and risk projections use distinct coordinates.
- **Three units, mean-value order.** Selecting A instead gives value 6.000 but top-set overlap .300; the strict
  report's risk is .4667. The top-set order in the table prefers B. Choosing a first recipient does not require
  publishing every comparison in a strict order.
- **Two units, τ .25.** The reporting optimum withholds. The added allocation lottery still fills a place,
  giving expected value 5.000 and overlap .500. It draws a whole subset of the required size from the boundary
  grade, rather than independently including each unit.
- **False-negative cost 3.** The native threshold classifier declares 2 positive, with cost .700. The convention
  “positive through the highest grade” declares only B positive and costs .900. Neither τ nor the place budget
  sets the probability cutoff for this decision. Under **Threshold 4**, being exactly at the substantive threshold does not count as above it. The native classifier
  declares 0 positive, at cost .300. The grade cutoff permits both none-positive and all-positive decisions: those actions remain
  distinct even if a canonical grade representation would lose the distinction.
- **Equal reporting risk, different classifications.** Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2, in A/B/C order, both have risk .2000. With the same
  added grade cutoff, they declare 3 and 2 positive, at costs 1.700 and 1.300. Equal reporting risk does not
  make the added actions equivalent.
- **League, five places.** Mean-score selection gives value .558 and estimated overlap 2.733. The top-set order
  gives estimated overlap 2.825. These membership probabilities use the displayed posterior draws; their ordering
  and overlap evaluation use the same draws.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
These are synthetic conditional laws. Value is the selected target value, rather than an intervention effect.
A grade-based allocation or classification requires a boundary lottery or an eligibility convention.
Finite-law quantities are exact; the league's normal means and threshold probabilities are analytic, while
membership and overlap are Monte Carlo estimates. The league reporting optimum covers only capped contiguous cuts
of its declared posterior-mean order; the strict comparison reports lie outside that family.
:::

Standalone: [one-place](../../embed/one-place.html), for example `?mode=threshold&falseNegativeCost=3`.

Related applications: [Restrictions imposed by a fixed order](order-misses.qmd), [The decision for an isolated pair](../grades/one-pair.qmd).
